title: Il faut, indefinites and adjective position
subtitle: il faut repeindre, tous les châteaux, un beau jardin
summary: Say what is necessary with il faut, use avoir besoin de and avoir envie de, quantify with quelques, plusieurs and tout, and put adjectives in the right place.

lesson.heading: Il faut = it is necessary
lesson.text: **Il faut** never changes - it has only the *il* form. Follow it with a **noun** (what you need) or an **infinitive** (what must be done). It often translates as *you need*, *we must* or *it needs*.

examples.note: You need a bit of light.

examples.text: Pour faire ce plat, **il faut** des tomates.
examples.note: To make this dish, you need tomatoes.
The flat needs repainting.

examples.text: Pour bien parler français, **il faut** connaître la grammaire !
examples.note: To speak French well, you have to know the grammar!

lesson.heading: Avoir + a noun without an article
lesson.text: Many everyday expressions use **avoir** + a bare noun where English uses *to be* or *to need*. **Avoir besoin de** (to need) is strong - it's essential. **Avoir envie de** means *to feel like* or *want*. Both take a noun or an infinitive, and *de* becomes **d'** before a vowel.

examples.note: I need money (to pay my rent).
He needs to rest.
We feel like a nice tart.

examples.text: Je **n'ai pas envie de** sortir, ce soir.
examples.note: I don't feel like going out tonight.
to be hungry, to be thirsty, to be sleepy

lesson.heading: Quelques, plusieurs - and tout
lesson.text: **Quelques** and **plusieurs** both mean *a few / several / a certain number of*. **Tout** on its own means *everything*; in the passé composé it goes before the participle.

examples.note: May I ask you a few questions?
She uses several dictionaries.

examples.text: **Tout** est sale ! **Tout** va bien ! Il comprend **tout** !
examples.note: Everything is dirty! Everything's fine! He understands everything!
I've read everything. They've sold everything.

lesson.heading: Tout le, toute la, tous les, toutes les (all the, the whole)
lesson.note: *Tout* agrees with the noun that follows it: *J'ai visité **toute la** région. Ils ont invité **tous les** garçons et **toutes les** filles.*

lesson.heading: Where does the adjective go?
lesson.text: Most adjectives go **after** the noun. A few short, very common ones go **before** it: *petit, grand, joli, beau, bon, mauvais, gros*. In careful French, **des** becomes **de** when the adjective comes before a plural noun.

examples.note: after the noun - the usual place

examples.text: un **petit** appartement, une **jolie** femme, un **grand** jardin
examples.note: before the noun

examples.text: un **bon** café, un **mauvais** film, un **gros** problème
examples.note: a good coffee, a bad film, a big problem
careful French; you will hear *des beaux* in conversation

lesson.heading: Irregular adjectives and plurals
lesson.note: Nouns follow the same plural rules: **-eau → -eaux** (*un château → des châteaux*) and **-al → -aux** (*un canal → des canaux*, *un journal → des journaux*). Most adjectives in *-al* do the same: *des exercices **oraux***. Before a masculine noun starting with a vowel, *beau* becomes **bel**: *un **bel** appartement*.

lesson.heading: Noun + à + infinitive
lesson.text: **À** + infinitive after a noun says what has to be done with it - like English *to rent*, *to do*. You see it in every property advert.

examples.note: a house for sale
a flat to rent
work to be done

examples.text: une pièce **à repeindre**, une voiture **à réparer**
examples.note: a room to repaint, a car to repair

exercises.prompt: Match each expression with its meaning.
Pour faire ce plat, ___ des tomates.
Does the adjective usually go before or after the noun?
Answer in the negative: *Est-ce que tu as besoin d'argent ?* — Non, ...
options: je ne suis pas besoin d'argent.
je n'ai pas un besoin d'argent.
exercises.explanation: **ne ... pas** goes around *ai*, and the expression stays **avoir besoin de**.

exercises.prompt: — Est-ce qu'ils ont faim ? — Non, ils ___ faim.
exercises.explanation: *Avoir faim* in the negative: **ils n'ont pas faim** - no article.
*Vieux* goes before the noun, and its feminine is irregular: **une vieille voiture**.

exercises.prompt: In careful French, which is correct? "We visited some beautiful castles."
options: Nous avons visité de beaux châteaux.
Nous avons visité des châteaux beaux.
Nous avons visité de belles châteaux.
Nous avons visité des beaus châteaux.
exercises.explanation: *Beau* goes before the noun, so **des → de**; *château* is masculine and *beau* → **beaux**.

exercises.prompt: Il y a un joli canal dans la ville ? — En fait, il y a plusieurs jolis ___ dans la ville.
exercises.explanation: Nouns in **-al** make their plural in **-aux**: *un canal → des canaux*.

exercises.prompt: Nous n'avons pas visité ___ châteaux de la Loire !
exercises.hint: tout le / toute la / tous les / toutes les

exercises.prompt: Il a passé ___ journée à jardiner.
exercises.hint: tout le / toute la / tous les / toutes les
exercises.explanation: *Journée* is feminine singular: **toute la journée** - the whole day.

exercises.statement: Toute le monde sait que la grammaire est importante.
exercises.explanation: *Monde* is masculine: **Tout le monde** sait que ...

exercises.prompt: Answer the question: *Tu vends un meuble ?* "Yes, I've got a piece of furniture to sell."
exercises.answer: Oui, j'ai un meuble à vendre.
